cta.p: When the whites or scrubs are done, replacements ship fast — boxed quantities for rotation.

pages.cardBlurb: Fat, wine, turmeric and scorch — the stain playbook that keeps whites white through a service week.
pages.h1: Washing chef whites: the stain playbook.
pages.metaTitle: Washing Chef Whites: Stains, Temperature & Routine | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to keep chef whites white — the pre-treat-by-stain playbook (fat, wine, tomato, scorch), the hot-wash routine, and when whites are honestly past saving.
pages.lede: Whites are the only uniform judged across a pass by customers who never see the wearer's face. Keeping them white isn't one trick — it's a routine plus a stain playbook, because fat, wine and turmeric all fight differently.

heroMeta.l: The rule that beats every product

steps.name: Scrape and pre-treat before the laundry bag
steps.text: Same-day treatment is the whole game — set stains are ten times the work. Degreaser on fat, cold water on protein, biological pre-treat on sauces.

steps.name: Wash hot with a biological detergent
steps.text: Whites tolerate what colours can't: wash at the hottest label temperature (commonly 60 °C or above) with a bio detergent whose enzymes eat food soils.

steps.name: Use oxygen bleach, not chlorine
steps.text: Oxygen-based whiteners lift greying safely; chlorine bleach yellows synthetics and weakens fibres — and is banned from most poly-cotton labels.

steps.name: Line-dry or tumble low, iron while damp
steps.text: Sun is a free mild bleach for cotton whites. Iron double-breasted fronts while slightly damp for the crisp finish that reads professional.

steps.name: Rotate three jackets minimum
steps.text: A jacket rested and properly washed outlasts one re-worn stained — rotation is what makes every other step possible.

blocks.html:
Every laundry product on the shelf loses to one habit: treating the stain the same day. Kitchen soils set with time and heat — a fat splash pre-treated after service shifts easily; the same mark after a hot wash and tumble is dyed in. So the routine is simple: scrape, pre-treat by stain type, hot bio wash, and never heat-dry a garment that's still marked (heat sets what the wash missed — the same rule as workshop oil).

Fabric matters too: cotton-rich whites tolerate the hottest washes and respond to sunlight; poly-cotton dries faster but yellows under chlorine bleach — which is why oxygen-based whiteners are the professional default.

faq.q: What temperature should chef whites be washed at?
faq.a: The hottest the care label allows — typically 60 °C or above for cotton-rich whites — with a biological detergent. Hot washing is what keeps hygiene-grade whiteness achievable; the label, not habit, sets the ceiling.

faq.q: How do you get grease out of chef whites?
faq.a: Pre-treat the same day with a degreaser or neat washing-up liquid, leave it 20 minutes, then hot wash. Never cold-wash a fresh grease mark first and never tumble-dry a garment still marked — both set the stain.

faq.q: Can you use bleach on chef whites?
faq.a: Oxygen-based whiteners, yes — they lift greying safely. Chlorine bleach is the wrong tool: it yellows poly-cotton, weakens fibres, and most whites' care labels prohibit it outright.

faq.q: Why do chef whites go grey?
faq.a: Accumulated soil and detergent residue from washes that were too cool, too short or overloaded — plus fabric fatigue. Regular hot bio washes with occasional oxygen-bleach soaks prevent it; once the base tone is grey despite the full routine, the garment is simply tired.

pages.cardBlurb: Home-washing clinical kit properly — the wash-separately, wash-hot, dry-fast routine and the policy line it follows.
pages.h1: Laundering scrubs: infection control at home.
pages.metaTitle: Laundering Scrubs for Infection Control | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to home-launder scrubs and clinical uniforms properly — separate wash, 60 °C benchmark, prompt drying, the change-at-work rule, and when items must go to industrial laundry.
pages.lede: Plenty of clinical and care staff launder their own uniforms — which makes the household washing machine part of the infection-control chain. The routine that keeps it sound is short, specific and worth doing exactly.

heroMeta.l: Damp kit grows what you washed off

steps.name: Bag it at work, transport it sealed
steps.text: Changed-out uniform travels home in its own bag — not worn on the commute, not loose with shopping. Policy usually says exactly this; it's the step most often skipped.

steps.name: Wash uniforms alone, promptly
steps.text: A separate load — no household mixing — as soon as practical. A waiting pile of worn clinical kit is the worst version of laundry.

steps.name: Wash at 60 °C where the garment allows
steps.text: The widely used benchmark for uniform decontamination. Modern scrubs are cut in poly-cotton rated for it — buy to that spec so the policy is washable.

steps.name: Dry completely, quickly
steps.text: Tumble or line-dry the same day. Prompt, complete drying finishes what the hot wash started; damp kit in a machine overnight undoes it.

steps.name: Iron or press if the fabric benefits
steps.text: Heat finishing adds a further margin on cottons — and a pressed tunic reads professional at handover.

blocks.h2: Home laundering is policy-permitted, not policy-free
blocks.html:
Most UK care providers and many NHS settings permit home laundering of everyday uniforms — within rules: change at work, transport sealed, wash separately at the stated temperature, dry promptly. The steps above are that consensus routine. Two hard exceptions sit outside it: visibly contaminated items (blood, body fluids) follow the employer's contaminated-linen process rather than a domestic machine, and theatre scrubs and specialist kit are industrially laundered, full stop.

The buying side makes the routine possible: scrubs or tunics rated for 60 °C washing, and enough sets that washing after every shift doesn't break the rotation.

faq.q: Can you wash scrubs at home?
faq.a: Usually yes for everyday uniforms, within policy rules: change at work, transport sealed, wash as a separate load at the stated temperature (60 °C is the common benchmark), and dry promptly and completely. Contaminated items and theatre kit are the exceptions — they go through the employer's process.

faq.q: What temperature kills bacteria on uniforms?
faq.a: The widely used benchmark for uniform laundering is a 60 °C wash with detergent — temperature and chemistry working together. Buy scrubs and tunics rated for it; a garment capped at 40 °C can't follow the policy it's worn under.

faq.q: Why can't scrubs go in with normal washing?
faq.a: Separation is the core control: it keeps clinical soils from circulating through household laundry and lets the uniform load run at the right temperature and cycle. It's the difference between laundering and just washing.
